(CNN) -- The economic downturn may take its toll at the 2009 Cannes Film Festival, which opens Wednesday night. But as always, the show will go on. Eli Roth and Brad Pitt are men on a mission in Quentin Tarantino's "Inglourious Basterds." Studios are cutting back on parties and all the glitz that goes with them, according to news reports. Moreover, there will be fewer people around to cover Cannes, as news organizations around the world trim costs. (Several, in fact, have tightened up by eliminating their movie reviewers.) Nevertheless, those who attend may see a bumper crop of good and intriguing films, Variety's Jay Weissberg told Reuters. "We've all been hoping Cannes would pull something out of the bag to make us feel good again. On paper, they have." Leah Rozen, film critic for People magazine, said there are several promising contenders for the Palme d'Or, Cannes' top prize, as well as a number of notable movies premiering out of competition. "What Cannes really is, is an international festival, and you really see world cinema," she said. "This year, there are 52 films that are going to be represented, of which 20 are in competition."  See Rozen talk about some of this year's promising works » . Two of the films in competition are American: Quentin Tarantino's World War II movie, "Inglourious Basterds," and Ang Lee's "Taking Woodstock," a tale about the 1969 music festival. Tarantino told The New York Times that he's been hoping to do a war movie for years. "You've got to make a movie about something, and I'm a film guy, so I think in terms of genres," he said. However, the maker of "Pulp Fiction" and "Jackie Brown" added, that doesn't mean what he ends up with resembles what he started with: "It's simply the spark that starts the fire." "Inglourious Basterds" was inspired by a 1978 Italian film that starred Bo Svenson ("Walking Tall, Part 2") and football player-turned-actor Fred Williamson ("Black Caesar"). Tarantino's film, which he characterized to the Times as "not a remake," stars Brad Pitt and Mike Myers. Cannes has been good to Tarantino; he won the Palme d'Or for "Pulp Fiction" 15 years ago. Buzz has been high on "Basterds" since Tarantino announced the project several years ago. "Taking Woodstock," the new film by "Brokeback Mountain" director Lee, is based on the book by Elliot Tiber, whose hotelier parents owned a musical festival permit in Bethel, New York, where Woodstock was held. The cast includes Liev Schreiber, Jeffrey Dean Morgan, Emile Hirsch, Imelda Staunton and Eugene Levy as Max Yasgur, on whose farm the festival was finally held. Other films in competition include Lars von Trier's "Antichrist," Jane Campion's "Bright Star" and Pedro Almodovar's "Broken Embraces."  Gallery: Some of Cannes' recent winners » . But this year's Cannes festival is attracting plenty of attention for its out-of-competition films as well. The festival is opening with "Up," the latest animated work from Pixar. "That sort of breaks convention to open with what is, basically, a fancy cartoon," Rozen said. Also at Cannes will be Heath Ledger's last film, "The Imaginarium of Dr. Parnassus." The Oscar-winning "Dark Knight" actor died during the making of the Terry Gilliam film; Gilliam managed to complete it by doing some rewriting and casting other actors -- including Jude Law, Colin Farrell and Johnny Depp -- to play Ledger's part. Despite the interest in seeing Ledger, the film is still struggling to find a buyer, though Entertainment Weekly recently reported that a Los Angeles screening went over well. Cannes, which also functions as a huge film marketplace, may widen the net in attracting distributors. But much of the fun from Cannes comes from the films that emerge from nowhere. Recent winners of the Palme d'Or include 2000's "Dancer in the Dark," which established singer Bjork as an actress, and "4 Months, 3 Weeks and 2 Days," a Romanian film that ended up topping many critics' lists in 2007. "One thing that always surprises me is that some of the films you have the lowest expectations for turn out to be terrific, and sometimes the bigger films turn out to be disappointments," Rozen said.

While the global economic downturn may cast a shadow over the 2009 Cannes Film Festival, opening Wednesday night, the show will inevitably go on. 

Amid tightening budgets, studios are paring down lavish parties and grand revelry, while news organizations worldwide trim coverage costs—with some even eliminating dedicated movie reviewers entirely. Yet, despite these austerity measures, attendees may well be treated to a remarkably rich crop of films. As *Variety*’s Jay Weissberg noted to Reuters, "We've all been hoping Cannes would pull something out of the bag to make us feel good again. On paper, they have."

Leah Rozen, film critic for *People* magazine, highlighted the festival’s strong roster of Palme d’Or contenders alongside a compelling slate of out-of-competition premieres. "What Cannes really is, is an international festival, and you really see world cinema," Rozen observed, noting that this year’s lineup features 52 films representing global cinema, 20 of which are competing for the festival's top prize.

Among the competing entries are two high-profile American features: Quentin Tarantino’s World War II movie *Inglourious Basterds*—starring Brad Pitt, Eli Roth, and Mike Myers—and Ang Lee’s *Taking Woodstock*. 

Tarantino returns to the festival 15 years after winning the Palme d’Or for *Pulp Fiction*, bringing a project that has generated intense buzz since its announcement several years ago. Inspired by a 1978 Italian film starring Bo Svenson (*Walking Tall, Part 2*) and football player-turned-actor Fred Williamson (*Black Caesar*), Tarantino clarified to *The New York Times* that his vision is "not a remake," but rather the realization of a longstanding desire to craft a war feature. "You've got to make a movie about something, and I'm a film guy, so I think in terms of genres," the director explained, adding that the genre is "simply the spark that starts the fire."

Meanwhile, Oscar-winning director Ang Lee presents *Taking Woodstock*, adapted from Elliot Tiber’s memoir about his hotelier parents, whose music festival permit in Bethel, New York, made the legendary 1969 event possible. The ensemble cast includes Liev Schreiber, Jeffrey Dean Morgan, Emile Hirsch, Imelda Staunton, and Eugene Levy as Max Yasgur, on whose farm the festival was ultimately hosted.

The international competition is equally formidable, featuring Lars von Trier’s *Antichrist*, Jane Campion’s *Bright Star*, and Pedro Almodóvar’s *Broken Embraces*.

Significant interest also surrounds this year’s out-of-competition lineup. In an unconventional move, the festival opens with Pixar’s latest animated feature, *Up*. "That sort of breaks convention to open with what is, basically, a fancy cartoon," Rozen remarked. 

Also featured out of competition is *The Imaginarium of Doctor Parnassus*, marking the final onscreen performance of the late Heath Ledger. Following the Oscar-winning actor's tragic death during production, director Terry Gilliam completed the film through narrative adjustments and by casting Johnny Depp, Jude Law, and Colin Farrell to complete Ledger’s role. Although a recent Los Angeles screening reportedly went over well, the film is still seeking a distributor. Cannes, which functions as a massive film marketplace alongside its festival slate, may help expand its reach to prospective buyers.

Ultimately, much of the allure of Cannes lies in its potential for unexpected discoveries. Landmark past Palme d’Or winners—such as 2000’s *Dancer in the Dark*, which established singer Björk as an accomplished actress, and 2007’s Romanian drama *4 Months, 3 Weeks and 2 Days*, which topped numerous critics' end-of-year lists—demonstrate the festival's unpredictable nature. 

As Rozen reflected, "One thing that always surprises me is that some of the films you have the lowest expectations for turn out to be terrific, and sometimes the bigger films turn out to be disappointments."

**CANNES, France (CNN)** — As the sun rises over the French Riviera, the world’s most prestigious film festival is preparing to roll out the red carpet. But as the 62nd Cannes Film Festival kicks off on Wednesday, it faces a unique balancing act: pairing Hollywood glamour and auteur heavyweights with the reality of a global economic downturn. 

For the next 11 days, the famous Boulevard de la Croisette will transform into the epicenter of the movie universe, packed with A-list celebrities, paparazzi, film buyers, and cinephiles vying for a glimpse of cinematic history.

This year’s festival opens with an unprecedented choice: Disney/Pixar’s 3-D animated feature "Up." Directed by Pete Docter, it marks the first time an animated film—and the first in 3-D—has held the coveted opening-night slot. While the selection raised a few eyebrows among traditionalists, festival director Thierry Frémaux defended the choice, calling it a testament to the evolving artistry of modern cinema.

"Animation has reached a peak of technical and emotional perfection," Frémaux told reporters ahead of the opening. "Starting with 'Up' is a signal that Cannes is open to all forms of great storytelling."

### A heavyweight clash for the Palme d'Or

Beyond the 3-D glasses and family-friendly opening, the main competition lineup reads like a who’s-who of international cinema giants, setting up one of the most fiercely anticipated battles for the Palme d'Or in recent memory.

High on the list of crowd-pleasers is Quentin Tarantino’s long-gestating World War II epic, "Inglourious Basterds." Starring Brad Pitt as the leader of a Jewish-American squad targeting Nazis, the film brings high-octane Hollywood star power to the Palais des Festivals. Tarantino, who won the Palme d'Or in 1994 for "Pulp Fiction," is expected to draw the festival’s largest crowds.

He faces stiff competition from festival favorites, including:

*   **Pedro Almodóvar**, returning with his noir-tinged romance "Broken Embraces," starring his longtime muse Penélope Cruz.
*   **Lars von Trier**, bringing his provocative psychological horror film "Antichrist," starring Willem Dafoe and Charlotte Gainsbourg.
*   **Ang Lee**, taking a sharp turn into comedy with "Taking Woodstock," a look at the generation-defining 1969 music festival.
*   **Jane Campion**, the only female director to ever win the Palme d'Or (for "The Piano" in 1993), returning with the romantic period drama "Bright Star."
*   **Michael Haneke**, presenting his haunting pre-WWI drama "The White Ribbon."

### Tightened belts on the Riviera

While the star power remains undiminished—with Pitt, Cruz, Dunst, and Gainsbourg all expected on the steps—the shadow of the global financial crisis looms over this year's proceedings. 

Industry insiders expect a leaner, more cautious festival. Major studios have scaled back their notoriously lavish beach parties, and film buyers are expected to be far more conservative with their wallets at the concurrent Marché du Film (Cannes Film Market). 

"The days of reckless midnight bidding wars are temporarily on hold," said veteran film analyst Marc Daniels. "Execs are looking for sure bets or low-budget gems. The belt-tightening is real, even in Cannes."

### Huppert leads the jury

Deciding who takes home the festival's top prize on May 24 is a nine-member jury headed by acclaimed French actress Isabelle Huppert. Known for her uncompromising performance choices, Huppert is expected to demand rigor and artistic vision from the competing films. Her fellow jury members include American actress Robin Wright Penn, British director Andrea Arnold, and American filmmaker James Gray.

As the final light checks are made and the famous red carpet is unrolled down the steps of the Palais, the festival promises a potent mix of high art, pop culture, and cinematic history. 

Whether 2009 will be remembered for 3-D revolution, Tarantino's swagger, or a dark horse discovery, one thing remains certain: for the next fortnight, all eyes in the movie world are on Cannes.

**Austerity on the Riviera, Magic on the Screen: 2009 Cannes Film Festival Prepares to Defy Global Recession**

**CANNES, France** — As the 62nd Cannes Film Festival prepares to roll out its iconic red carpet this week, the usual glitz and glamour of the French Riviera face an unprecedented shadow. The global economic crisis has finally reached the Boulevard de la Croisette, forcing Hollywood studios, independent distributors, and international news outlets to tighten their belts. Yet, while the legendary late-night parties may be scaled back and champagne flutes half-full, the festival’s artistic core remains fiercely intact. Cannes 2009 is shaping up to deliver one of the most potent, star-studded, and critically exciting film lineups in recent memory.

### Less Beluga, More Business: The Recession Bites the Croisette

There is no masking the financial anxiety hanging over this year’s gathering. Following the collapse of major financial institutions and a worldwide credit crunch, the lavish excess that has long defined Cannes is taking a mandatory hiatus. 

Floating megayachts are fewer in number along the harbor, and several major American studios have slashed their marketing budgets. The extravagant, million-dollar beach parties hosted by major distributors—a staple of the festival’s promotional machine—have either been downsized or canceled altogether. News organizations, hit hard by declining ad revenues and print layoffs, are sending significantly smaller contingents of journalists and critics, with many opting to cover the festival remotely.

The anxiety extends to the *Marché du Film* (the Cannes Film Market), the industry’s central hub for buying and selling movie rights. With independent film financiers struggling to secure capital, industry insiders expect a cautious, slow-moving market. "It's a year of sobriety," noted one veteran foreign sales executive. "People are here to do real business, not to pop 500-euro bottles of champagne on the beach."

### A Vintage Lineup Rescues the Show

If the economic climate is bleak, the silver screen promises pure escapism and high-stakes cinema. Festival General Delegate Thierry Frémaux has assembled a breathtaking slate that proves that while money may be tight, creative vision is in surplus. 

Making history right out of the gate, the festival will open with Pixar’s **"Up,"** directed by Pete Docter. It marks the first time in Cannes history that an animated feature—and a 3D film—has been selected for the prestigious opening-night slot. The poignant story of an elderly widower flying his house to South America via thousands of balloons promises to bring both technical innovation and emotional warmth to a somber global mood.

The main Competition slate reads like a who’s-who of world cinema royalty, anchored by some of the biggest names in modern filmmaking:

*   **Quentin Tarantino’s "Inglourious Basterds":** Unquestionably the most anticipated premiere on the Croisette, Tarantino returns to the scene of his 1994 *Pulp Fiction* triumph. Starring Brad Pitt as the leader of a squad of Jewish-American soldiers inflicting brutal retribution on Nazis in occupied France, the film promises high-octane revisionist history, trademark dialogue, and instant box-office buzz.
*   **Ang Lee’s "Taking Woodstock":** Stepping away from the heavy drama of *Lust, Caution* and *Brokeback Mountain*, Oscar-winner Ang Lee brings a lighter, nostalgic energy to the Competition. The film dramatizes the true story of Elliot Tiber, the man who helped enable the legendary 1969 music festival. Its sun-drenched, feel-good vibe might be precisely what recession-weary audiences are craving.

### Bittersweet Farewells and Heavyweight Contenders

Beyond the Competition for the coveted Palme d'Or, one of the festival's most emotionally charged moments will occur Out of Competition with the screening of Terry Gilliam’s fantastical **"The Imaginarium of Doctor Parnassus."** 

The film is forever etched in tragedy as the final performance of **Heath Ledger**, who died mid-production in January 2008. In a moving tribute to the late actor, friends Johnny Depp, Jude Law, and Colin Farrell stepped in to complete Ledger’s unfinished scenes, playing transformed versions of his character. Cannes audiences will finally get to witness Ledger’s parting gift to cinema—a performance early reports describe as captivating and whimsical.

The rest of the program is equally packed with heavyweight auteurs. Austrian master Michael Haneke will unveil his chilling pre-WWI drama *The White Ribbon*; Lars von Trier is set to shock audiences with his controversial horror-drama *Antichrist*; Pedro Almodóvar returns with the noirish drama *Broken Embraces*, starring Penélope Cruz; and Jane Campion—the only female director ever to win the Palme d'Or—presents *Bright Star*, a biopic about poet John Keats. 

### Cinema Prevails

As festival-goers polish their tuxedos and adjust to a leaner Riviera experience, the 2009 edition of the Cannes Film Festival serves as a reminder of the industry's resilience. The lavish parties may be muted, and the press corps trimmed, but when the lights go down in the Palais des Festivals, the power of storytelling remains untouched.

Cannes may be pouring a little less Dom Pérignon this year, but on the screen, a rich vintage awaits.

The French Riviera is rolling out its iconic red carpet this week for the 62nd Cannes Film Festival, but as the champagne chilled along the Boulevard de la Croisette, a sobering reality hung over the palm trees: the global economic meltdown has officially arrived in cinema’s holy land.

In previous years, Cannes was synonymous with unbridled extravagance—giant yachts docked in the bay, million-dollar beach parties hosted by indie distributors, and wild bidding wars for untested scripts. This year, the party budgets have been slashed, the yachts are noticeably smaller, and studio executives are flying coach. With major specialty divisions like Warner Independent and Picturehouse shuttered over the past year, the independent film market that thrives in Cannes is facing its toughest climate in decades.

"There's no question the mood on the business side is cautious, even anxious," says veteran film critic Leah Rozen of *People* magazine. "The days of buyers throwing around insane money over beluga caviar are on hold. Hollywood is feeling the pinch, and the market here is going to reflect that belt-tightening."

Yet, if the financial forecast is cloudy, the artistic line-up for Cannes 2009 is blindingly bright.

In a historic move, the festival will open Wednesday evening with Pixar’s *Up*—marking the first time in Cannes history that an animated film, and a 3-D one at that, has snagged the prestigious opening-night slot. Attendees in tuxedos and evening gowns will don plastic 3-D glasses inside the Palais des Festivals, signal-boosting Disney’s massive summer push while offering a colorful, family-friendly antidote to the real-world economic gloom.

Beyond the animated sky, the competition for the coveted Palme d’Or reads like an auteur dream team, packed with previous winners and heavy-hitting cinema titans. 

The most anticipated storm on the Croisette is undoubtedly Quentin Tarantino’s long-gestating World War II epic, *Inglourious Basterds*. Starring Brad Pitt as the leader of a squad of Jewish-American soldiers hunting Nazis, the film is making its world premiere in competition, exactly 15 years after Tarantino brought home the Palme d'Or for *Pulp Fiction*.

"Tarantino brings instant electricity whenever he steps onto the Riviera," Rozen notes. "When you bring Brad Pitt to Cannes with a violent, wildly stylish war movie, people are going to forget about the stock market for two hours. That’s the magic of this festival—the sheer star power can eclipse the balance sheet."

Tarantino is hardly the only heavy hitter competing for the top prize, overseen this year by Jury President Isabelle Huppert. Spanish master Pedro Almodóvar returns with the noirish melodrama *Broken Embraces*, starring Penélope Cruz. Austrian director Michael Haneke brings his stark historical drama *The White Ribbon*, while Ang Lee offers a lighter touch with the 1960s-set *Taking Woodstock*. 

Meanwhile, provocateur Lars von Trier is already sending shockwaves through the festival circuit with *Antichrist*, a psychological horror film starring Willem Dafoe and Charlotte Gainsbourg that is rumored to feature some of the most intense, controversial imagery seen on the Croisette in years.

Add to the mix Terry Gilliam’s out-of-competition fantasy *The Imaginarium of Doctor Parnassus*—featuring the final, tragic performance of the late Heath Ledger—and the 2009 festival promises no shortage of emotional and cinematic fireworks.

For an industry reeling from a year of studio downsizing and tightened budgets, the next 11 days offer a crucial reminder of why the movies matter. The market may be subdued, but the art form is flexing its muscles.

As Rozen puts it: "We might be drinking sparkling wine instead of Dom Pérignon on the beach this year, but once the lights go down in the theater, the movies look just as rich as they ever did."
